overview: Cost-consequence analysis of a pathway change in a regional pain service, comparing all percutaneous spinal cord stimulator trial episodes started in 2026 (in-person day 3 visit) with those started in 2027 (structured nurse telephone review on day 3), from the health service and patient perspectives.
population: All adults starting a percutaneous spinal cord stimulator trial between 1 January 2026 and 31 December 2027; about 88 episodes a year. Episodes are analysed in the pathway of their start date whatever the patient chose on day 3.
exposure: 2027 pathway: a nurse telephone review on day 3 with a wound and symptom checklist and a same-day clinic slot when anything is flagged; in-person day 3 remains available on request. 2026 pathway: an in-person day 3 clinic visit. Both keep the in-person day 8 review and lead removal.
procedures: Resource use per episode is taken from the pain service records (contacts, same-day reviews, extra visits), the hospital emergency department system (attendances within the trial week and 30 days after lead removal) and theatre records (re-siting or early removal). Unit costs come from finance memo FIN-PM-2026-14. Patient and companion costs are estimated for both years from postcode distance, a per-kilometre rate and the proportion of companions losing a working day; in 2027 a short optional questionnaire at day 8 checks the estimate.

outcomes.name: Health service cost per trial episode
outcomes.measure: Sum of costed contacts, same-day reviews, extra clinic visits, emergency attendances and unplanned procedures from lead placement to 30 days after lead removal, 2026 prices
outcomes.timing: Per episode, analysed at the end of 2027
outcomes.why: The manager's question; directly affected by the pathway.

outcomes.name: Patient and companion cost per trial episode
outcomes.measure: Travel, out-of-pocket and lost working time, estimated from postcode distance
outcomes.why: Likely the larger share of the change (claim c4).

outcomes.name: Permanent implant decision made on the planned day
outcomes.measure: Proportion of episodes with the decision recorded at the day 8 review
outcomes.why: The trial exists to reach this decision; a delay is a real consequence for patients.

outcomes.name: Unplanned attendance during the trial week
outcomes.measure: Any unscheduled clinic or emergency attendance between lead placement and removal
outcomes.why: The main risk of removing a visit (claim c1).

outcomes.name: Trial-related infection within 30 days
outcomes.measure: Infection recorded in pain service or emergency records within 30 days of lead removal
outcomes.why: Infections appear late and are reported by patients (claim c2); they must not be missed.

outcomes.name: Telephone review duration and trigger rate
outcomes.measure: Minutes per call and proportion of calls leading to a same-day review

feasibility: About 176 episodes over two years from existing records; four protected hours a week cover extraction of about four episodes an hour after the first month.
biasMitigation: Pre-specified list of resource items and unit costs before 2027 data are looked at
The same postcode method for patient costs in both years
Case-mix comparison (age, diabetes, lead type) and a sensitivity analysis restricted to single-lead trials
Co-interventions recorded on a dated log

biasFlags.label: Historical comparison
biasFlags.note: Other changes between the years may explain differences; the log and sensitivity analysis limit this.

biasFlags.label: Unrecorded patient costs in 2026
biasFlags.note: Estimated, not measured; the same estimation in both years keeps the comparison fair.

biasFlags.label: Rare consequences
biasFlags.note: Reported as counts with intervals, not tested.

flags: Two balancing measures and one process measure are descriptive
parsimony.simplestPath: One comparison of two years, one primary cost outcome, consequences listed beside it.

theoreticalFramework: No behavioural framework; the analysis follows the cost-consequence format with CHEERS 2022 reporting.
summary: Two-year cost-consequence comparison with one primary cost outcome, two secondary outcomes, two balancing measures and one process measure.
